events.headline: Thirsty farms, slowing turbines: how depleting dams threaten power, harvest

items.title: Thirsty farms, slowing turbines: how depleting dams threaten power, harvest
items.summary: India’s depleted reservoirs are threatening agriculture and hydropower after one of the driest monsoon seasons in decades. Rabi planting has fallen behind last year, with wheat, rice and pulses acreage down.

events.article_text:
Scanty rains of the southwest monsoon have left India’s key reservoirs severely depleted, threatening irrigation, agricultural output and hydropower generation. Reservoirs that were over 90% full last year are now not even two-thirds full, official data showed, following one of the driest monsoon seasons in decades.

Water levels at India’s 178 reservoirs supplying irrigation canals, hydropower units and municipal drinking water are down 27% from a year ago to 121.9 billion cubic metres (bcm), official data showed. The dry spell is already rippling through the rural economy, where six states have declared drought, rabi crop sowing has dropped, and the Reserve Bank of India has warned of mounting risks to food inflation.

Apart from the central region where levels were marginally above last year’s, storage was lower in all other regions, data from the Central Water Commission showed.

The water scarcity was worst in the southern region, where reservoirs are only 42.6% full (against last year’s 89.97%), compared with north having 56.62% (86.32%), west 76.17% (96.10%), east 75.74% (81.66%) and central 84.23% (92.01%). While the southwest monsoon that brings most of India’s rains has concluded, the northeast monsoon remains active in the southern peninsula, raising hopes of further rains in catchment areas.

Not surprisingly, sowing has slipped. Crops were sown across 11.7 million hectares till 6 November, 2.43 million hectares below last year’s 14.1 million at this time. To be sure, rabi sowing is still on, and typically continues till end of December. India’s average rabi acreage in the FY21 to FY25 period was 70.1 million hectares.

Less water for irrigation may impact sowing and harvest, experts pointed out.

“Low reservoir levels, particularly in the western and southern regions, could affect rabi crop cultivation, as farmers in these areas depend heavily on reservoir water for irrigation. Crops such as wheat, paddy, pulses and oilseeds could face irrigation constraints if water availability remains limited during critical growth stages,” said Sudhir Panwar, a farm policy expert and former member of Uttar Pradesh Planning Commission.

Wheat acreage has slipped 12% to 1.97 million hectares, rice 3.10% to 673,000 hectares, and pulses 14.4% to 3.2 million hectares, agriculture ministry data showed.

However, some said the impact will be limited in the northwestern region.

“The impact of lower reservoir levels on rabi crops is likely to be negligible in northwestern India, as the region is well-irrigated. Moreover, wheat, a major rabi crop in the region, requires relatively less water and all the growing areas are irrigated. The impact is likely to be concentrated in areas where farmers depend heavily on reservoir water for irrigation,” said AK Singh, former director, Indian Agricultural Research Institute (ICAR).

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warned in September that the 2026 El Niño could be unprecedented in strength, potentially taking Pacific Ocean temperatures 3.8°C above average, with its peak expected towards the end of 2026 and climate impacts extending well into 2027. For India, it means below-normal rainfall, higher temperatures and prolonged drought conditions. India’s southwest monsoon rainfall in 2026 stood at 87% of the 50-year average, making it the fourth-lowest since 2001 and the 13th-lowest since 1901, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD). October rainfall saw a deficit of 31.4%.

In late October, Maharashtra expanded drought relief to 305 of the state’s 358 talukas and approved a ₹7,500-crore package, including ₹5,000 aid for eligible farmers.

While coal dominates India’s power sector, hydropower plays a critical role in supporting solar and wind power. Turbines can be quickly turned on and off; so, hydropower can step in or dial down when the sun doesn’t shine and the wind doesn’t blow.

“In the case of run-of-the-river hydro projects, the lesser discharge of water may impact hydropower generation and the decline in reservoir levels would also bring hydro power generation below what is generally witnessed during these months,” said Raj Kumar Chaudhary, former chairman and managing director, NHPC Ltd.

India has 20 reservoir-based hydropower projects, monitored by the CWC. Gobind Sagar dam in Himachal Pradesh, with a generation capacity of 1.3GW as of 5 November had storage of 56.87% of the full reservoir level (FRL), compared to 85.09% in the corresponding period last year. It is also way below its 10-year average of 73.52%. Similarly, the reservoir level in the Koyna dam (1.9GW) in Maharashtra is currently at 87.67% of the full reservoir level, while last year it stood at 100%. The current level in Tehri dam (1GW) in Uttarakhand is 92.91%, compared to 95.28% last year.

Chaudhary added that heating demand may add to overall consumption. The former NHPC chief noted that although solar and thermal would play a key role in these winter months, pollution and heavy smog in northern states could impact solar power generation in the region, affecting overall power supply.

“Thermal power generation is expected to be adequate, and in states like Rajasthan, solar power generation should help. But in Delhi-NCR and neighbouring areas, instances of pollution, smog and cloud cover may reduce solar power generation. That may hit overall solar generation,” he said.

This year, India witnessed a record power demand of 270.8GW in May, and instances of shortfall during peak demand hours also reached multi-year highs of 30 million units a day in September. Experts suggested that despite the fall in decline, such high shortfalls may not be seen in the winters.

Queries mailed to the ministry of jal shakti, power, NHPC and SJVN remained unanswered till the press time.

analysis.tldr: Drying reservoirs threaten to hike food prices and squeeze farm incomes, which could strain household budgets across India.
the_story: Scanty southwest monsoon rains left India's key reservoirs down 27% from a year ago to 121.9 billion cubic metres, with six states declaring drought.
Water scarcity is worst in the southern region (42.6% full) and western region (76.17% full), while rabi crop sowing dropped to 11.7 million hectares compared to 14.1 million hectares last year.
Wheat acreage slipped 12%, rice dropped 3.10%, and pulses fell 14.4% according to agriculture ministry data.
Lower water discharge is hitting hydropower generation, which helps back up solar and wind power, while winter smog in northern states may further cut solar generation.
analysis.what_happened: Scanty rains during the southwest monsoon season caused water levels in India's 178 key reservoirs to drop significantly compared to last year. This lack of water has reduced irrigation for winter crops and slowed down hydropower generation, driven by dry spells and deficient rainfall.
analysis.analogy: It is like a family water tank running dangerously low during summer, forcing you to ration water for your kitchen garden while also worrying about electricity bills because your backup generator is running dry.
why_it_matters_india: Scanty monsoon rains cause reservoir water levels to drop sharply across regions like the south and west.
Farmers face water shortages, leading to a drop in the planting of winter crops like wheat, rice, and pulses.
Lower crop output reduces supply, which pushes up food prices and increases food inflation for regular households.
Reduced water flows also cut hydropower generation, raising stress on the overall power supply network.

impacts.rationale: Lower crop production due to water scarcity drives up food prices, which is bad for everyday household budgets.
Fewer crops sown and harvested mean lower earnings for farmers, hurting rural spending.

watch_next: Progress of the northeast monsoon rains in the southern peninsula
Updates on rabi crop sowing acreage by the end of December
analysis.caveats: Better-than-expected winter rains or strong irrigation in well-watered northwestern regions could lessen the impact on final crop yields.

analysis.tldr: When global metal prices drop due to a stronger US dollar, raw materials for Indian factories become cheaper, but it also signals slowing world demand that can hurt global trade.
the_story: Base metals are losing momentum because of a strong US dollar and worries about demand.
The Dollar Index (DXY), which measures the US dollar against other major currencies, has climbed to the 103-104 range.

This dollar strength is driven by strong US economic data, high Treasury yields (interest rates paid by the US government), and expectations that the Federal Reserve (US central bank) will keep interest rates high for a longer period.
analysis.what_happened: Prices of base metals are falling. This is happening because the US dollar has grown stronger, pushed up by positive US economic reports and the expectation that American interest rates will stay high. When the dollar is strong and US interest rates are attractive, global investors pull money into US assets, putting pressure on commodity prices.
analysis.analogy: It is like a strong magnet (the US dollar) pulling metal filings away from everywhere else, leaving the actual piles of metal sitting around with fewer buyers bidding for them.
why_it_matters_india: The US Dollar Index climbs to the 103-104 range due to strong US economic data and high interest rate expectations.
Global commodities like base metals are priced in US dollars, making them more expensive for buyers using other currencies, which dampens demand.
Lower global metal prices reduce input costs for Indian manufacturing and engineering companies that import raw metals.
However, falling metal demand globally can signal a cooling world economy, which eventually affects Indian export earnings and global market sentiment.

impacts.rationale: A strong US dollar naturally pressures other currencies down, making imports slightly costlier for regular people.

impacts.target: Indian metal company stocks (like Tata Steel, Hindalco)
impacts.rationale: Falling global base metal prices mean lower selling prices for metal producers, which can hurt their profit margins.

watch_next: Movements in the US Dollar Index (DXY)
Updates from the US Federal Reserve on future interest rate decisions
analysis.caveats: The provided text was mostly website promotional filler with only a single headline and short snippet about base metals, limiting deep specific context.

analysis.tldr: When everyday items become expensive due to supply shortages rather than too much money in the economy, raising interest rates loses its power to fix the problem, meaning your loans may stay costly without successfully lowering prices.
the_story: Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran stated that adjusting interest rates is becoming less effective at controlling inflation because of supply chain disruptions.
He pointed out that fiscal policies (government spending and tax rules) will play a crucial role in tackling these supply-driven challenges.
Nageswaran noted that many countries have struggled to meet their inflation targets since 2022.
He warned that supply shocks could dominate inflation dynamics over the long term.
analysis.what_happened: India's Chief Economic Advisor warned that traditional central bank tools—like raising borrowing costs—cannot easily fix price rises caused by broken supply chains or shortages of goods. When the root cause is a lack of physical goods rather than too much public spending, raising interest rates fails to bring prices down effectively.
analysis.analogy: It is like trying to fix a traffic jam by locking the gas station doors; if the road is physically blocked by fallen trees, stopping cars from buying fuel will not clear the path.
why_it_matters_india: Supply disruptions push up the cost of raw materials and everyday goods in India.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI, India's central bank) finds its interest rate hikes less effective at lowering these specific prices.
This leaves the heavy lifting to the government's fiscal policies (budget and spending decisions) rather than just central bank rate cuts or hikes.
If interest rates stay high longer to fight stubborn inflation, consumer loans and EMIs (Equated Monthly Installments, fixed monthly loan payments) remain expensive for ordinary people.

impacts.rationale: Persistent supply shocks mean everyday costs stay elevated, which is bad for household budgets.
If rate hikes fail to cool inflation quickly, borrowing costs may stay higher for longer, making home and car loans expensive.

watch_next: Government budget announcements for measures targeting supply chains
Future statements from the Reserve Bank of India on interest rate decisions
analysis.caveats: Global supply chains could suddenly heal faster than expected, reducing pressure on domestic prices without requiring major government intervention.

events.headline: Iran War Accelerates Southeast Asia’s Renewable Energy Push

items.title: Iran War Accelerates Southeast Asia’s Renewable Energy Push
items.summary: Several countries in Asia have recognised the need to accelerate the deployment of renewable energy to reduce reliance on fossil fuel imports and support energy diversification. events.article_text:
Trump Extends Jones Act Waiver For Another 90 Days

Felicity Bradstock is a writer and journalist based in Mexico City. She writes for energy websites and covers several other industries, as well as writing…

Several countries in Asia have recognised the need to accelerate the deployment of renewable energy to reduce reliance on fossil fuel imports and support energy diversification.

The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has significantly reduced fuel trade in recent months, leading to fears of shortages as countries worldwide scramble to find different suppliers and switch to alternative energy sources. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has previously pointed out the significant potential Asia has to increase its renewable energy capacity, and now several governments are putting the agency’s advice into action.

An October report published by the IEA stated that “Southeast Asia’s energy security challenges are intensifying as demand grows, reliance on imported fuels rises, and interactions across energy systems become increasingly complex – creating a greater need for coordination and planning.” In the report, the IEA recommends stronger national preparedness and deeper regional cooperation in energy to help the region overcome ongoing supply disruptions and volatile prices.

Over the last decade, energy demand per person in Southeast Asia has risen by nearly 30 per cent, driven by economic growth, industrial development, and urbanisation. Meanwhile, the region’s crude oil output has decreased by 40 per cent since its 1990s peak, driving up oil imports. The region has also increased the import of liquefied natural gas (LNG) in recent years, leaving it highly vulnerable to price fluctuations and trade disruptions.

The IEA predicts that electricity demand in Southeast Asia will increase by around 5.4 per cent per year between 2026 and 2030, driven by greater use of cooling, expanding industries, and the growth of data centres. Meeting the growing demand will require significant investment in the region’s grids, new generating capacity and system flexibility. The review therefore recommends that Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) countries diversify their sources and routes of supply, make greater use of domestic energy resources where economically viable, and expand energy efficiency and electrification.

Fuel shortages and high prices, driven by the war in Iran that began in February, have prompted several Asian governments to focus on expanding renewable energy capacity to strengthen energy security. Between February 28 and August 31, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Vietnam, and the Philippines announced 37 renewable energy and electrification policies and 29 fossil fuel policies. Some of these measures were already under consideration before the war began.

According to an investigation by Zero Carbon Analytics, most of Southeast Asia’s new fossil fuel policies focus on short-term relief, with implementation periods of less than six months, while the majority of renewable energy and electrification policies target long-term change. Of the 37 renewable energy and electrification policies announced, 24 have implementation periods of around three years or more, compared to just six of the 29 fossil fuel policies.

Renewable energy capacity across the Asia-Pacific region, excluding China, is expected to expand by more than 840 GW between 2026 and 2031, more than doubling the capacity added during the previous six-year period. The expansion would bring the region’s total installed renewable energy capacity to almost 1,700 GW by 2031, according to the IEA’s latest Renewables 2026 report. India is expected to account for nearly half of the capacity growth, followed by Southeast Asian countries, which are forecast to contribute around 20 per cent of the increase.

The IEA has revised its renewable energy capacity forecast for the Asia-Pacific region upwards by 15 per cent, or 87 GW, compared with last year's projections for the overlapping 2026–2030 period. Stronger solar photovoltaic deployment in India, South Korea, Indonesia and Australia has outweighed weaker expectations for wind and hydropower. The agency has also raised its forecasts for the Philippines and several other regional markets, while revising expectations for Japan and Chinese Taipei downwards.

Despite the improved outlook, the IEA highlighted several ongoing challenges facing renewable energy development, including inadequate grid infrastructure, financing difficulties, permitting delays and land acquisition problems. These issues are particularly significant in Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam, where governments have strengthened renewable energy policies but continue to face difficulties translating targets into operating projects. Greater investment in electricity grids, energy storage and system flexibility will be essential to support further expansion.

Solar photovoltaic installations are expected to account for almost 80 per cent of renewable energy capacity additions across the Asia-Pacific region, excluding China, between 2026 and 2031, followed by onshore wind at 12 per cent and hydropower at 7 per cent. Competitive auctions are expected to drive more than half of utility-scale renewable capacity growth. The region is also forecast to remain the world's second-largest hydropower growth market, although delays to conventional hydropower projects in India and Vietnam have prompted a modest downward revision. However, India's pumped-storage hydropower outlook has improved, reflecting the growing need for energy storage and grid flexibility as solar and wind capacity expands.

The ASEAN region is expected to see a sharp acceleration in renewable energy deployment through 2031, with solar photovoltaic installations leading the expansion. The IEA expects stronger rooftop solar incentives, expanded installation quotas and improved access to corporate power purchase agreement

analysis.tldr: Middle East conflicts and shifting global energy markets mean India must accelerate its own massive push into solar and green power to manage import costs.
the_story: The ongoing war in Iran, which began in February, has disrupted fuel trade in the Middle East and triggered fears of fuel shortages worldwide.

Between February 28 and August 31, Southeast Asian nations like Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Vietnam, and the Philippines announced 37 renewable energy policies and 29 fossil fuel policies.
A report by the International Energy Agency (IEA) predicts that electricity demand in Southeast Asia will jump by about 5.4 per cent per year from 2026 to 2030.
Renewable energy capacity across the wider Asia-Pacific region, excluding China, is projected to grow by over 840 GW (gigawatts, a measure of power generation) between 2026 and 2031.
India is expected to drive nearly half of this upcoming renewable capacity growth in the Asia-Pacific region.
analysis.what_happened: Middle East conflicts have disrupted traditional oil and fuel supplies, prompting countries across Asia to scramble for alternative energy sources. As a result, governments are fast-tracking long-term renewable energy policies like solar power to reduce their heavy reliance on imported fossil fuels.
analysis.analogy: It is like a household seeing the price of delivered cooking gas spike uncontrollably due to supplier fights, deciding to finally install rooftop solar panels so they stop getting caught in sudden price shocks.
why_it_matters_india: Middle East conflict causes fears of oil supply shortages -> global energy markets become volatile and prices fluctuate.
Asian nations including India accelerate their transition to solar and renewable infrastructure to secure independence from imported fuels.
India is projected to account for nearly half of the entire Asia-Pacific region's renewable capacity growth through 2031.
Massive domestic green energy expansion requires huge investments in electrical grids and equipment like solar panels and storage.

impacts.target: Renewable energy stocks in India (like solar equipment makers and green utilities)
impacts.rationale: Strong regional and domestic focus on solar growth creates massive business opportunities for Indian clean energy firms, which is generally good for investors in these sectors.
Middle East conflict disrupts fuel trade and supplies, making oil costlier — a negative for everyday consumers and importers like India.
Pricier imported fuel and energy drive up everyday transportation and goods manufacturing costs, which hurts household budgets.

watch_next: Updates on the IEA's regional renewable capacity forecasts and solar installation quotas
Progress on India's domestic grid infrastructure and pumped-storage hydropower projects
analysis.caveats: Supply chain bottlenecks, financing difficulties, and land acquisition problems could slow down how quickly these planned renewable energy projects actually get built.

events.headline: Early warning must also reach farmers without institutional support [Commentary]

items.title: Early warning must also reach farmers without institutional support [Commentary]
items.summary: For India, an El Niño year has usually meant a weaker monsoon. That relationship is a tendency rather than a rule, and there have been El Niño years that ended with normal rain, but the odds move, and they move against us. This year the signal was unusually emphatic. The India Meteorological Department put the […]

events.article_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

For India, an El Niño year has usually meant a weaker monsoon. That relationship is a tendency rather than a rule, and there have been El Niño years that ended with normal rain, but the odds move, and they move against us.

This year the signal was unusually emphatic. The India Meteorological Department put the probability of El Niño developing during the monsoon season at 92%. The United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration gave it a 96% chance of persisting through the coming winter, and several analyses placed it in the ‘super El Niño territory’, comparable in strength to 2015. IMD’s seasonal outlook was for rainfall at 90% of the long period average, with a 60% likelihood that the season would close with a deficit.

The monsoon followed the warning, and Rajasthan felt it early. By the first week of September, the state was 21% short of normal rainfall, with 21 of its districts deficient and only two in surplus. That put the state in step with a country that recorded a 13.8% shortfall between June and August, and where cumulative rainfall stayed about 15% below the long period average through September. Elsewhere the deficit has already turned into formal declarations, as in Maharashtra, which has declared drought in 265 of its 358 talukas.

However, in the fields, the signal came earlier than any declaration. Nationally, kharif sowing lagged by about 16% on July 10, at 53.12 million hectares against 63.27 million a year earlier. Sowing recovered through July and August, but the rain did not. That gap is the lesson of this season. Every El Niño year will bring deficits and declarations, and it will also bring a forecast months in advance.

The question worth asking is not whether the country knew what was coming, but whether the farmers who had to act on that knowledge received it in a form they could use, before the loss rather than after it. In Rajasthan, where drought is a recurring hazard rather than an exception, that question is sharpest. That led us to our investigation.

The forecast that reached farmers is the output of a system India has spent nearly five decades building. At the forecasting end, the science has improved steadily and performs well. The larger difficulty lies in the last stretch, between the bulletin and the field, which is the dissemination.

Drought early warning in India rests largely on the Agromet Advisory Services, which were set up in 1977, when IMD began issuing state-level bulletins through All India Radio and the newspapers, the only channels with sufficient rural reach at the time. Doordarshan followed, with programmes such as Krishi Darshan. All of it was one-way, generalised and tied to a broadcast schedule. The service was brought down to the district level in 2008, restructured under the Gramin Krishi Mausam Sewa, and extended to the block level in 2018 in partnership with the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR). More than 130 Agromet Field Units and a network of District Agromet Units housed at Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) now generate the advisories.

What a farmer is meant to receive is not a single alert but a sequence that sharpens as the season approaches. At the longest range, six to eight months out, IMD’s Multi-Model Ensemble and its statistical forecasting system indicate the broad character of the coming monsoon. This is where an El Niño signal first enters the system. Medium-range bulletins, issued twice a week, convert five-day forecasts into specific farm operations such as ‘hold back sowing’, ‘delay the irrigation’, ‘bring the harvest forward’. Short-range warnings for sudden events reach phones in near real time.

The delivery has changed more than the science. Where a bulletin once travelled by radio and newsprint, it now moves through SMS, WhatsApp groups run by Krishi Vigyan Kendras, applications such as Meghdoot, the Kisan Portal, and the social media accounts of state agriculture departments. On paper this is a considerable advance: from generic and delayed to targeted and immediate.

Between May and August this year, we spoke with farmers across the geographic zones of Rajasthan, one of India’s historically most drought-exposed states. Half had sustained contact with their local Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) and used digital advisory channels actively. The other half had no such institutional link with a KVK. The two groups differed in how they received the advisories and in how they responded to El Niño.

Among the first group, the El Niño warning did precisely what an early warning system is supposed to do. It arrived early enough to change the shape of the kharif.

“It was an El Niño year, so I didn’t sow the rice all at once. I watched which way the rain was going and sowed it in portions, one section at a time,” said Rampal, a farmer from Sri Ganganagar.

Others changed the crop itself, moving away from anything thirsty.

“This year I didn’t sow crops that need a lot of water. Instead I sowed bajra and guar, because they need less water,” said another farmer Sheeshpal from Pratapgarh. “This year I didn’t plant soybeans. I sowed bajra (pearl millet) in its place,” said Rajpal, a farmer from Baran.

One farmer described something more precise than crop substitution, a calculation that set the advisory against his own irrigation capacity and left him a deliberate margin. In his 25-bigha land, he sowed ten. If the rain failed, the tube well could carry that much; and he had saved the cost of sowing the other fifteen.

Among the second group, the same season in the same districts, under the same advisory zone, produced a different account entirely.

“We are relying on god. We have sown the crop and are waiting for the rain, and the crop is being ruined,” said Girdhari, a farmer from Jaisalmer. This brings us to a striking contrast i.e. one infrastructure and one season, yet opposite outcomes.

analysis.tldr: When poor monsoon rains hurt crop production, everyday food prices in India can rise and rural spending power can drop.
the_story: The India Meteorological Department predicted a 92% chance of an El Niño weather pattern (a climate phenomenon that usually brings weaker monsoons to India) with rainfall expected at 90% of the long-term average.
Actual rainfall fell short, leaving Rajasthan with a 21% deficit by early September and Maharashtra declaring drought in 265 of its 358 talukas (sub-districts).

Farmers with active links to institutional advisory networks (like Krishi Vigyan Kendras) successfully adapted by staggering sowing, switching to water-efficient crops like bajra and guar, or planting on less land.
Farmers without these institutional links had no guidance, relied purely on hope, and watched their crops get ruined.
analysis.what_happened: An El Niño weather pattern triggered poor and delayed monsoon rains across India, leading to severe rainfall shortages and drought declarations in states like Maharashtra and Rajasthan. While India has built a multi-decade forecasting system to warn farmers months in advance via SMS, apps, and local units, farmers without institutional links missed out on these crucial advisories and suffered heavy crop losses.
analysis.analogy: It is like having a weather app on your phone warning of a massive storm, but if your phone has no internet connection, you step out into the rain completely unprepared while your neighbor stays dry inside.
why_it_matters_india: Poor monsoon rains lead to lower agricultural output and failed harvests.
Lower crop production reduces food supplies, causing retail food inflation (rising prices for everyday groceries) to climb.
Distressed farmers and rural communities see their incomes drop, reducing their spending power on consumer goods.
Lower rural demand can weigh on the overall economic growth and corporate earnings of companies that sell goods in villages.

impacts.rationale: lower crop yields due to drought make food items more expensive, which is bad for household budgets

impacts.target: FMCG (fast-moving consumer goods) stocks like Hindustan Unilever & ITC
impacts.rationale: when farmers earn less from failed harvests, they buy fewer daily household products, hurting company sales

impacts.target: Rural wage growth and job demand
impacts.rationale: drought reduces farming activity, leaving rural workers with fewer jobs and lower incomes

watch_next: Final government crop production estimates for the kharif (summer) season
Updates on reservoir water storage levels across different states
analysis.caveats: The provided text cuts off mid-sentence, leaving out final conclusions, but the core reporting on El Niño impacts and the digital divide among farmers remains clear.

analysis.tldr: Efforts by China to reduce reliance on the US dollar could eventually reshape global trade currencies, potentially influencing how Indian businesses and the government pay for imports like oil.
the_story: Panelists on a Council on Foreign Relations episode examined China's efforts to reduce its dependence on the U.S. dollar and build alternatives to the dollar-centered system.

Experts assessed the progress and limits of these efforts, including the internationalization of the renminbi (China's currency, also known as the yuan) and the development of alternative payment systems.
The panel also looked at China's growing financial ties with emerging markets and what these changes mean for the future of U.S. financial power.
The discussion was hosted by Edward Fishman and featured guests Martin Chorzempa, Robert Greene, and Jess Hoversen.
analysis.what_happened: Experts at a policy discussion analyzed how China is trying to bypass the U.S. dollar in global trade by promoting its own currency and setting up new payment networks. This is happening as China builds deeper financial connections with developing countries to reduce its reliance on American-led financial systems.
analysis.analogy: It is like two major grocery stores trying to get local shoppers to use their own store vouchers instead of the town's universally accepted cash, hoping to control how people buy and sell over time.
why_it_matters_india: China pushes to use its own currency, the renminbi, for global trade ->
Countries begin exploring payment systems that bypass the U.S. dollar ->
Global trade habits shift very slowly over years, affecting how international commodities are priced ->
India has to carefully balance its trade payments and currency stability as global financial habits evolve.

impacts.rationale: If global dollar dominance is questioned long-term, currency markets could see broad shifts, though this specific discussion does not trigger an immediate move.
Any disruption in how global oil and imports are settled can indirectly affect import costs, which impacts everyday household expenses.

analysis.tldr: New RBI rules could make it harder for big private investment funds to control multiple non-bank lending companies, which might slow down fast-paced lending but make the financial system safer for everyone.
the_story: India's central bank (the RBI, which regulates the country's banks and money) is working on new rules to stop private equity firms (PE firms, which are private investment funds that buy stakes in companies) from holding controlling stakes in multiple non-bank lenders (financial companies that give loans but are not traditional banks).
The proposal aims to reduce financial risks that come from global PE investments in India.
Under the plan, larger stakes will face heavier checking and scrutiny, but smaller investments will still be encouraged to help the financial sector grow.
Recent data shows there has been heavy foreign investment in these non-bank lenders, showing high demand for credit (loans) in the country.
analysis.what_happened: The RBI is planning strict new rules for private equity firms because a lot of global money has been flowing into India's non-bank lenders. The central bank wants to prevent a situation where a few private investment groups control too many lending companies at once, which can create hidden risks for the whole financial system.
analysis.analogy: It is like a parent stopping one single person from buying and driving a fleet of school buses all at once — smaller investments are like letting people own a few seats, but letting one outsider steer multiple buses creates too much risk for the passengers.
why_it_matters_india: RBI drafts rules to stop private equity firms from controlling multiple non-bank lenders ->
Global investment funds face tighter checks and scrutiny when buying large stakes in these financial companies ->
Non-bank lenders might find it slightly harder to raise massive chunks of private equity money quickly ->
The overall financial system becomes safer from sudden shocks, protecting everyday depositors and borrowers.

impacts.rationale: Stricter rules on who can buy and control them could slow down their aggressive growth, which might temporarily weigh on their stock prices — a mixed signal for equity investors.
Fewer hidden risks from heavily concentrated ownership mean a safer banking and lending environment for the whole country — good for overall economic health.

watch_next: Official guidelines or draft circulars released by the RBI detailing the exact ownership limits
How private equity firms react to the proposed restrictions regarding their existing investments
analysis.caveats: The article is based on an early media report about rules being worked on, and the final policy details from the RBI could look different when officially announced.

events.headline: Past weather trends show fewer cyclones crossing Tamil Nadu coast during Northeast monsoon

items.title: Past weather trends show fewer cyclones crossing Tamil Nadu coast during Northeast monsoon

events.article_text:
Published - November 15, 2026 01:00 am IST - CHENNAI

Senior meteorologists point out that only 22 of the 117 cyclonic systems that formed over the Bay of Bengal during October and November, between 1981 and 2025, made landfall along the State’s coast. | Photo Credit: VELANKANNI RAJ B

Tamil Nadu has seen relatively fewer cyclonic systems crossing its coast during the Northeast monsoon in the past 45 years, noted meteorologists.

The Bay of Bengal is churning its next cyclone for the season. However, the current predictions indicate the possibility of only less rainfall over the State.

Many of the systems moved northwards towards places such as Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, West Bengal, Bangladesh and the Arakan coast, while others weakened over the sea without crossing any coast.

Y.E.A. Raj, former deputy director general of meteorology, Regional Meteorological Centre, Chennai, said 68 of the 117 systems moved north of Tamil Nadu towards the neighbouring States or countries, while 26 dissipated over the Bay of Bengal without making landfall. However, the State has received rainfall during some past years when the system dissipated over the sea.

Citing IMD data, he said of the three to four weather systems or cyclones that generally form over the Bay of Bengal between October and December, only one comes closer to or crosses the Tamil Nadu coast.

Going by statistics since 1981, Tamil Nadu experiences a coastal crossing roughly once every two years during October and November. The occurrence of three weather systems moving north of Tamil Nadu during October and November is not unprecedented. A similar pattern was recorded in 10 previous years, including 1983, 1996, 2010 and 2013, Mr. Raj added.

analysis.tldr: Historical weather trends show that fewer cyclones cross the Tamil Nadu coast, which generally lowers the risk of widespread storm damage and sudden crop disruptions for the local economy.
the_story: Between 1981 and 2025, only 22 out of 117 cyclonic systems that formed in the Bay of Bengal during October and November made landfall (crossed from sea to land) along the Tamil Nadu coast.
Y.E.A. Raj, a former deputy director general of meteorology, noted that 68 of those systems moved north toward Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, West Bengal, Bangladesh, and the Arakan coast.
Another 26 systems simply dissipated (weakened and disappeared) over the sea without hitting any coast.

Data from the IMD (India Meteorological Department) shows that while three to four weather systems generally form in the Bay of Bengal between October and December, only one usually nears or crosses Tamil Nadu.
analysis.what_happened: Meteorologists analyzed past weather data from 1981 to 2025 and found that the vast majority of cyclonic storms forming in the Bay of Bengal during the Northeast monsoon miss the Tamil Nadu coast. Instead, they shift northward toward other states and countries or die out over the open ocean.
analysis.analogy: It is like a bowling alley where most balls thrown down the lane veer off to the side or run out of momentum before hitting the pins at the end of the specific target lane.
why_it_matters_india: Fewer cyclones hitting Tamil Nadu lowers the immediate risk of severe property damage and agricultural loss in the state.
This historical pattern helps local authorities and farmers better prepare, knowing that heavy storm strikes are statistically less frequent than northward-moving systems.
Even when storms weaken over the sea, past years show the state can still receive beneficial rainfall without the destructive winds.
Lower overall cyclone frequency reduces emergency relief spending and supply chain disruptions for goods produced in the region.

impacts.target: Tamil Nadu agricultural crop prices (like rice and vegetables)
impacts.rationale: Fewer destructive cyclones mean crops are less likely to be ruined, keeping local food supplies stable and prices from spiking—which is good for household budgets.

impacts.target: Local property insurance claims in coastal Tamil Nadu
impacts.rationale: Fewer landfalls mean fewer damaged homes and businesses, resulting in lower insurance payouts and potentially more stable insurance costs for residents.

watch_next: Updates from the IMD (India Meteorological Department) on the current season's developing cyclone in the Bay of Bengal
Rainfall measurements across Tamil Nadu to see if storms weakening over the sea still bring helpful water
analysis.caveats: Historical trends do not guarantee what any single upcoming storm will do, as changing climate patterns can always create unexpected weather paths.

history.title: The AAA company that could not pay
history.what: IL&FS, an infrastructure lender rated AAA weeks earlier, missed payments on its short-term borrowings. India's entire non-bank lending sector froze within days, and debt mutual funds holding its paper had to mark down investors' money.
history.why: It borrowed short-term at low rates to fund infrastructure that would pay back over decades — a maturity mismatch that works perfectly until the day nobody rolls over your short-term borrowing. Its group ran to roughly 350 subsidiaries, which made the true debt load nearly impossible to see from outside. And the rating agencies that called it AAA were paid by it.
history.impact: Non-bank lenders' funding costs jumped. Housing finance companies stopped lending, which hit developers, which hit construction jobs. This is a large part of why Indian growth slowed through 2019, well before Covid. Several debt funds gated withdrawals.
history.policy: The government superseded the board. The RBI brought large non-bank lenders under far closer supervision, imposed liquidity coverage requirements on them, and limited how much short-term money they could rely on. SEBI tightened what debt funds were allowed to hold.
history.consequence: Indian non-bank lending is meaningfully safer and slower than it was, and credit-risk funds never recovered their popularity. It also drove consolidation: weak lenders were absorbed and the survivors, mostly bank-backed, took the market.
history.pattern: Maturity mismatch is the oldest failure in finance, and a credit rating is an opinion bought by the borrower. When an institution borrows short to lend long, the question is not whether it is profitable but who refinances it on a bad day.
history.india_echo: This is India's own 2008 in miniature, ten years later. It is why the bad-loan line matters more for Indian banks than any valuation ratio.
history.watch_for: Any lender whose borrowings are much shorter-dated than its loans, and any AAA rating sitting on a complicated group structure.
